translations.text: Herod sent and seized John: and so on.
Mark the Evangelist wrote in the book of Christ about the great Baptist John, that "the cruel king Herod seized him and put him in prison because of his brother's wife Herodias": and so on.
This John was the greatest of men, as Christ bore witness about him. He said, "Among those born of women there has arisen no greater man than John the Baptist."
You have often heard about his great way of life and his ministry; now we wish to give you some explanation concerning the interpretation of this gospel.
This Herod, who ordered John to be beheaded, and who at the Saviour's passion gave his consent to the governor Pilate and handed him over to his judgement, was the son of the other Herod,
who reigned at the time when Christ was born. But it was customary at that time for powerful men to give their children names after themselves,
so that the father would seem to be remembered all the more when the son, his heir, was called by the father's name.
The cruel father, Herod, left five sons; he had ordered three of them killed during his mortal illness, before he departed.
That Herod died cruelly and suddenly after he had killed the children because of Christ's birth. Then his son Archelaus succeeded to the kingdom.
Then, about ten years later, he was driven from his royal throne, because the Jewish people accused him of his pride before the emperor, and the emperor then sent him into exile.
Then the emperor divided the Jewish kingdom into four and set four brothers over it. In the Greek language these are called tetrarchs, that is, rulers of a fourth.
A tetrarch is one who holds the fourth part of a kingdom. One of these brothers was called Philip, and he married the daughter of Aretas, king of the Arabian people; she was called Herodias.
Then after some time they fell out, Philip and Aretas, and Aretas took his daughter away from his son-in-law and gave her to Philip's brother Herod,
because Herod had greater fame and power. Herod then cast off his lawful wife and adulterously lived in a wicked marriage.
At that time John the Baptist was preaching God's righteousness to all the Jewish people, and he rebuked Herod for that foul marriage.
The Ecclesiastical History tells it thus: When Herod saw that the whole Jewish multitude was flocking to John's teaching and eagerly obeying his admonitions, he became afraid,
and thought that because of John's teaching they would reject his kingship. He wanted to forestall this, and he put John in prison in a fortress called Machaerus.
Then John sent two disciples from the prison to Christ and asked him, saying, "Are you the one who is to come, or should we wait for another?"
It is as if he said, "Show me whether you yourself will go down to the dwellers in hell for the redemption of mankind, just as you were willing to be born for the redemption of mankind;
Or, if I am to announce your coming to those in hell, just as I proclaimed to the world that you were coming, make it clear.
Then at that same hour, as Luke the Evangelist wrote, the Saviour healed many sick people of various diseases, gave sanity to the mad, and gave sight to the blind;
and afterwards he said to John's messengers, "Go now to John and tell him the things that you have seen and heard."
See, now the blind see, and the lame walk, and lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, and the dead rise, and the poor preach the gospel; and blessed is he who is not offended in me."
It was as if he said to John: Such wonders I work, but even so I will suffer death for the redemption of mankind, and follow you in dying,
and blessed is he who now praises my wonders, if he does not despise my death, and does not, because of that death, lose faith that I am God.
Thus the Saviour revealed to John that he would humble himself to death, and afterwards visit the inhabitants of hell.
Then, meanwhile, it happened that Herod, as we said before, feasted his counsellors on the day on which he was born; for at that time they held great rejoicing on their birthdays.
The daughter then, as we said before, danced with her maidens at the banquet, to the pleasure of them all, and the father then promised with an oath that he would give her whatever she desired.
We have heard of three impious sins: the unhappy celebration of his birthday, the wanton leaping of the girl, and the father's rash oath.
It is fitting for us to oppose these three things in our conduct.
We must not turn our birthday into any feast-day with idle celebrations, nor hold our birth in such remembrance;
but we must get ahead of our last day with repentance and penance, as it is written, "In all things be mindful of your last day, and you will never sin."
It is not fitting for us to disgrace our body, which has been hallowed to God in the saving baptism, with unseemly play and frivolity;
for our bodies are God's limbs, as Paul said, "And he commanded that we should prepare our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God."
The body is a living sacrifice that is shielded against deadly sins, and through holy virtues is acceptable to God and holy.
God himself forbids every oath to Christian men, saying thus, "Do not swear by heaven, for it is God's throne.
Do not swear by the earth, because it is God's footstool.
Do not swear by your own head, because you cannot make a single hair of your head white or black.
I say to you, Do not swear by anything, but let your speech be ended thus: It is as I say, or it is not so."
Whatever goes beyond that by way of an oath comes from the evil one."
Christ himself confirmed his speech, when he spoke to a Samaritan woman, with these words, "Crede mihi":

that is, "Believe me." Nevertheless, if we anywhere swear unwarily, and the oath compels us to a worse deed, then it is more advisable for us to avoid the greater guilt, and to make amends to God for the oath.
Indeed David swore by God that he would slay the foolish man Nabal, and destroy all his possessions;
but at the first intercession of the wise woman Abigail, he put his sword back into its sheath, and praised the woman's wisdom, which had prevented him from that perilous manslaughter.
Herod swore through folly that he would give the dancing daughter whatever she asked:

Then, because he did not want his fellow guests to call him a perjurer, he mixed the feast with blood, and gave the death of the great prophet to the wicked dancing-girl as a reward for her entertainment.
It would have been much better for him to break the oath than to order such a prophet to be killed.
In all things we must carefully take heed, if we ever, through the devil's snares, fall into two dangers at once, that we always flee the greater guilt by way of escape through the lesser,
just as one does who wishes to escape from his enemies over a wall: he looks for where the wall is lowest, and leaps over there.
Truly Herod, when he would not, at John's admonition, give up the unclean marriage, then fell into manslaughter;
and the lesser sin was the cause of the greater, so that for the sake of his foul adultery, which he well knew was hateful to God, he shed the blood of the prophet, who he knew was pleasing to God.
This is the sentence of the divine judgement, concerning which it is said, "He who does harm, let him do harm still more; and he who dwells in filthiness, let him defile himself still more."
This sentence befell the cruel Herod. Now there is another sentence briefly spoken concerning good men: "He who is holy, let him be sanctified still more."
This befell John the Baptist, who was holy through manifold merits; and he was sanctified still more when, through preaching the truth, he came to a victorious martyrdom.
Herod pretended to be sad when the daughter asked him for the head;
but he rejoiced in secret, because she asked for the death of the man whom he had already wanted to kill, if he had had a pretext.
for truly, if the girl had asked for the woman's head, he would have refused her in great anger.
John was not forced by persecution to deny Christ, but he still gave his life for Christ when he was martyred for the sake of truth.
Christ himself said, "I am the truth." John was Christ's forerunner in his birth and in his preaching, in baptism and in suffering, and he went before him to the dwellers in hell by a precious death.
When he had been beheaded, his disciples came and carried his holy body to a city called Sebaste, and they laid him there. The holy head was buried in Jerusalem.
Some heretics said that the head was supposed to blow upon the king's wife Herodias, on whose account he was killed, so that she was carried by the winds throughout the whole world;
but they were wrong in that tale, because she lived out her life to its end after John was slain.
In truth, John's head was afterwards revealed to two eastern monks who had come to visit the city to pray, and from there they carried the precious treasure to a certain city called Edessa;
and Almighty God revealed countless miracles through that head. After a long time his bones were brought to the famous city of Alexandria, and laid to rest there with great honour.
Now we must consider how Almighty God allows his chosen and beloved servants, whom he has predestined to eternal life, to be destroyed and crushed with such great torments in this present life.

But the apostle Paul answered this, saying that "God chastens and scourges everyone whom he receives into his kingdom, and the more shamefully a man is punished for God's name, the greater his glory is before God."
Again the same apostle said in another place, "The sufferings of this time are not to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us."
Now the commentator says that no wild beast, whether four-footed or creeping, can be compared with an evil woman.
What among four-footed beasts is fiercer than the lion? Or what among the serpent kind is more cruel than the dragon?
But the wise Solomon said that it would be better to live with a lion and a dragon than with a wicked and talkative woman.
Truly, John lived in the wilderness unharmed among every kind of beast, among dragons and asps and every kind of serpent, and they feared him.
But the accursed Herodias killed him by beheading, and received the death of so great a man as a reward for her daughter's dancing.
The prophet Daniel lay unharmed for seven nights among seven lions in a pit, but the accursed woman Jezebel deceived the righteous Naboth to his death through false witness.

The prophet Jonah was kept undigested in the whale's belly for three nights, but the treacherous Delilah deceived the strong Samson with flattery, and once his hair was shorn she betrayed him to his enemies.
Therefore no kind of serpent and no kind of wild beast is equal in wickedness to an evil woman.

The historian Josephus wrote, in the ecclesiastical history, that the cruel Herod ruled his kingdom for only a little while after John's death; because of his crimes, first his army was slain in battle,

and afterwards he himself was driven from his kingdom and sent into exile. This was a very just judgment: since he would not listen to John's teaching about eternal life, he also quickly and shamefully lost his temporary kingdom.
Augustine the wise admonishes us with these words, saying, "Consider carefully, I beg you, my brothers, how miserable this present life is;
and yet you fear that you will leave it too soon. You love this life, in which you live with toil;
you worry about your needs; you run about and are troubled; you plough and sow and gather in again; you grind and bake;

you weave, and work to get clothing, and you can hardly keep count of all your needs, both at sea and on land; and you must bring all these things just mentioned, and your own life too, to an end in hardship.
So learn now, that you may know how to earn eternal life, in which you will suffer none of these toils, but will reign with God for ever."
In this life we grow faint if we do not sustain ourselves with food; if we do not drink, we are overcome with thirst; if we stay awake too long, we grow faint;
If we stand for long, we grow tired, and then we sit; then again, if we sit too long, our limbs go to sleep. Consider also, after this, that our body has no stable state:
childhood passes into boyhood, and boyhood into full-grown stature; full-grown stature bends toward old age, and old age is ended by death.
Truly our life-span has no stability, but as much as the body grows, by that much its days are lessened.
Everywhere in our life there is exhaustion, weariness and decay of the body, and yet everyone wishes to live long. What is living long but toiling long?
Few people in these days are granted to live eighty years in good health, and whatever anyone lives beyond that,
it is toil and pain for it, as the prophet said, "Our days are evil," and they are all the worse the more we love them.
In this way this world flatters very many people, so that they do not want their miserable life to end. True and blessed life is when we rise from death and reign with Christ.
In that life there are good days, yet not many days but one, which has no dawn and no ending; no following day comes after it, because no yesterday came before it;
but that one day is eternal, never ending, without any night, without afflictions, without all the toils that we listed a little earlier in this reading.
This day and this life are promised to righteous Christians. May the merciful Lord lead us to it, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever without end. Amen.
